segments.text: At one point, BlackBerry was one of the most powerful names in smartphones. So how did it lose its place in the market?
BlackBerry built its reputation on secure messaging, physical keyboards, and business communication. By 2009, it held almost 20 percent of the global smartphone market.
Then the market changed. Apple's iPhone introduced a new kind of smartphone experience, while Android brought touchscreen devices to a growing range of manufacturers.
BlackBerry struggled to respond quickly enough. It underestimated how much consumers valued large touchscreens, broader app ecosystems, and a different mobile experience.
The consequences were enormous. BlackBerry's global smartphone unit market share fell from around 20 percent in 2009 to almost nothing by 2016.
BlackBerry eventually stopped developing its own phone hardware and shifted its focus toward software, cybersecurity, and secure communications. The company didn't disappear. It changed what it was.
Here's the lesson: your biggest advantage today can become your biggest weakness tomorrow. Success requires more than protecting what works. It requires adapting before the market leaves you behind.
